source_title: Tyriq Withers Bares His Abs and His Soul for Sexiest Man Alive (Exclusive) - People.com
source_excerpt:
“I’m just extremely grateful. Hopefully we can just keep this train going,” says the ‘Reminders of Him’ actor
Tyriq Withers is the fashion world’s latest It guy, but his style journey began during his childhood in Jacksonville, Fla.
“My mom always made sure I went to school in a coordinated outfit,” the actor, 28, says on the set of his Sexiest Man Alive shoot in Los Angeles in August. “Middle school was when I really started to step out with the all-white skinny jeans, a snapback, Hollister T-shirts and Vans. I always took fashion very seriously. Was it good? I don’t know.”
These days Withers is more likely to step out in head-to-toe designer wear like at his first Met Gala in May, where he wore a custom Louis Vuitton outfit complete with a sheer shirt and crystal-studded jacket.
“Quite the shift,” quips the actor, who’s also not afraid to rock a man-bag.
“I’m trying to get a little Birkin,” he says, before adding with a laugh, “I’m not in that tax bracket.”
Just give it time. After a breakout moment in Atlanta in 2020, Withers has been quickly climbing the Hollywood ladder with hit films like the I Know What You Did Last Summer reboot and Jordan Peele’s Him . He most recently starred in the March romance Reminders of Him .
“Between all the press and premieres and films coming out, it’s been a year of firsts,” he says. “I’m just extremely grateful. Hopefully we can just keep this train going.”
Here, Withers discusses his career rise, staying grounded and his goals of having a mini-me in the future.
We already know you took fashion very seriously as a kid. How else would you describe little Tyriq?
I was super pale and I had a big head and my nickname was Casper, so that’s going to be my kid’s first name, whenever that may be — 10, 20 years from now.
I took school very seriously, and I played a lot of soccer. That was my life: soccer and academics. Not to brag or anything, but I graduated number seven in my class. 4.63 GPA, 4.0 unweighted GPA. Very important. I think that was a route out for me. I wanted to be a neurosurgeon, because I watched Grey’s Anatomy . Then I realized, “He’s an actor.”
So, that’s when you knew you wanted to become an actor?
It was also the Disney Channel Games. Like, “How do I get there, mom? Wizards of Waverly Place , how do we do it?” That never happened, so I think the turning point for me was in college [at Florida State University]. I had kids in the film school [asking], “Be in my short film?” I got the bug for that there.
At the time, you were also playing as a walk-on wide receiver for the Florida State Seminoles. How did you balance it all?
I just hated sports at one point. I felt trapped and I needed to express this emotion, so I auditioned for a play and then I wiped my hands clean of sports and I really dove in. When COVID hit, that’s when it was full time, trying to figure it out.
When you booked Atlanta , how did that change everything for you?
I think at the time I didn’t understand the magnitude of how important that show is to the culture and the filmmaking community. It’s paramount to where I’m at today. Shout out to Donald Glover for directing that episode. It pushed my storytelling abilities, because I think when I was filming it, I was so ignorant to how the story could relate to anyone who struggles with identity. That episode specifically, for me, I was like, who’s going to relate to this niche experience? But I think the more niche a story is, the more universal it feels. So, I’m super grateful for Atlanta .
What would you say was the most memorable moment when you found out you got a role?
When I was auditioning for the movie, Him , I was in Serbia, shooting a movie, so I had to do everything over Zoom. I did a series of auditions. I filmed a highlight tape of me working out and throwing a football — and trust me, it is hard as hell to get an American football in Europe. They had one final call and they were like, “We want you to do some improv. We just want to see if you have the chops.” [Director] Justin Tipping is on the call and the producers, and then they’re like, “Hi, this is Jordan Peele. We don’t know if you know him.” I’m like, “Do I know Jordan Peele?” Then I go into an improv with the director, and in the middle of the improv, he’s like, “You got the part.” I’m like, “What? What are you talking about?” I remember I came out of the improv, and I started jumping around.
You’ve really gotten to dip your toes into a variety of genres.
Yeah. I think we’re all mosaics. We’re all an accumulation of our past experiences. And I think I have a lot to offer, whether it’s the quiet, yearning, brooding [character] or whether it’s the funny guy who’s really hiding a deep insecurity.
I always had a passion to really tell a plethora — SAT word — of stories, because I really resonated with comedy through Instagram sketches or YouTube sketches and I think that’s how I connected with people. The empath in me is like, “Oh, they’re laughing? My day is so much better.”
Trail mix, walking with a friend, music. I like other people’s favorite music. I’ll ask you what’s your favorite song, and then you’ll share your favorite song and I’m like, “Man, life is amazing, I love this song too.” The beach, having a cocktail or two, therapy. My friends will see me go into therapy like “Ugh,” and I’ll come out like a f---ing Phoenix.
I have a love-hate relationship with my girl, Mercedes. That’s my therapist’s name. I ghost her sometimes. She knows whenever I say, “Mercedes, get that schedule ready,” I’m in it. I’d say I’ve been with her about two years, but now we’re on a twice-a-week basis, because I need that.
My friends and family are tough on me, but they allow me space. I have this rule if you’re venting: Do you want to be helped, hugged, or heard? I used to get upset when I would vent and somebody would be immediately trying to fix it, and I’m like, “Uh-uh. I’m venting. When I regulate, you can give me advice on what I can do better.” I don’t want anybody to feel like they have to bulls--- to be around me.
You’re a Cancer and self-described “lover boy.” What’s the most romantic thing you’ve ever done?
I really liked this woman, and then I made her a bad-day box. I got this trunk, and I painted the outside with black-charcoal chalk paint. I gave her a marker to write on the outside, so whenever she’s in a good mood, she can talk to her future self who is in a bad mood like, “Hey, keep slaying.” Something like that.
Then, when she opened the box, it played her favorite song, “Lean Wit It, Rock Wit It.” I took the motor from a birthday card and I wired it. I put a jar of 50 Things I Love About You or... I can’t remember where we were in the relationship... “Like” About You, a journal, her favorite scents, a candle. I did the whole shebang. Lover boy. People are going to think, “Oh, he’s insane.” We’re not together anymore.
What does your perfect date night look like?
I pick you up. Make sure you’re wearing a sweatsuit and we go get lunch, your favorite restaurant, boom, after lunch we go paintball and we’re on opposite teams. And then if you beat me, we can continue this relationship. If I beat you, we can assess. What if we went and wrestled some pigs?
What do you think is the sexiest part of a woman?
I think the sexiest part about a woman is the resilience in a world where it’s not built for the advantages of a woman. I surround myself with strong women.
How did your late brother Kionte inspire you to want to become a dad? (Kionte died at 26 in a car crash in 2021.)
I used to get jealous because when he had his son, he was so soft and gentle. He used to bully the hell out of me. I saw the love he had for his son, and you could tell it filled a void that he had in lack of fatherly love.
I really was inspired — still inspired by it — because I think he’s still around and still in a sense helping raise my nephew even though he’s not physically here. I think spiritually, emotionally he’s around.
I’m sure he’d be proud of everything you’ve accomplished.
I think once I work with Michael B. Jordan , he’ll be proud. He was a tough critic. He was like, “ Ah , but let me know when MBJ is on set with you.”
When you think of your life and career 10 years from now, what do you envision?
Hopefully I’m still kicking. I want to be happy and keep pouring into my creative, storytelling bag. I want to have a whole life, a full life. I want to have a little mini-me, maybe two, three or four. Hopefully my rich-person life starts to hit by then, but not only financially…rich in friendship, rich in family — and rich in designer bags.
